claim: The visual cortex plays an important role in object detection.
source: Although the visual cortex plays an important role in object detection, the superior colliculus can support detection when the visual cortex is ablated or silenced.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific data from this manuscript.

claim: The superior colliculus can support detection when the visual cortex is ablated or silenced.
source: Although the visual cortex plays an important role in object detection, the superior colliculus can support detection when the visual cortex is ablated or silenced.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, drawing from prior research.

claim: Superficial layers of mouse SC (sSC) encode visual features of complex objects.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that superficial layers of mouse SC (sSC) encode visual features of complex objects, and that this code is not inherited from the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: The visual feature code in mouse sSC is not inherited from the primary visual cortex.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that superficial layers of mouse SC (sSC) encode visual features of complex objects, and that this code is not inherited from the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure contrast.
source: Here, we use optogenetics to show that mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure contrast, orientation, and phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure orientation.
source: Here, we use optogenetics to show that mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure contrast, orientation, and phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure phase.
source: Here, we use optogenetics to show that mouse sSC is involved in figure detection based on differences in figure contrast, orientation, and phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In mouse sSC, image elements that belong to a figure elicit stronger activity than those same elements when they are part of the background.
source: Additionally, our neural recordings show that in mouse sSC, image elements that belong to a figure elicit stronger activity than those same elements when they are part of the background.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: The discriminability of the neural code in sSC is higher for correct trials than for incorrect trials.
source: The discriminability of this neural code is higher for correct trials than for incorrect trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The primary visual cortex (V1) is involved in object detection and segregation.
source: The primary visual cortex (V1) is involved in object detection and segregation (e.g. Lamme, 1995; Ress et al., 2000; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Silencing or ablating V1 does not completely abolish the detection of simple visual stimuli in mice.
source: Silencing or ablating V1, however, does not completely abolish the detection of simple visual stimuli in mice (Prusky and Douglas, 2004; Glickfeld et al., 2013; Resulaj et al., 2018; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Humans with bilateral lesions of V1 remain capable of detecting some visual stimuli, even in the absence of conscious vision.
source: Furthermore, humans with bilateral lesions of V1 remain capable of detecting some visual stimuli, even in the absence of conscious vision; a phenomenon termed 'blindsight' (Ajina and Bridge, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The capacity for visual detection in the absence of V1 is likely to be mediated by the superior colliculus.
source: This capacity is likely to be mediated by the superior colliculus (SC), a sensorimotor hub in the midbrain (Tamietto et al., 2010; Kato et al., 2011; Ito and Feldheim, 2018; Kinoshita et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and represents an inference from those studies.

claim: The SC receives direct input from the retina, as well as from V1 and other sensory areas.
source: The SC receives direct input from the retina, as well as from V1 and other sensory areas (Basso and May, 2017), and mediates orienting responses to salient stimuli in primates and rodents (White and Munoz, 2012; Allen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The SC mediates orienting responses to salient stimuli in primates and rodents.
source: The SC receives direct input from the retina, as well as from V1 and other sensory areas (Basso and May, 2017), and mediates orienting responses to salient stimuli in primates and rodents (White and Munoz, 2012; Allen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In mice, detection of change in isolated visual stimuli is impaired in a space- and time-specific manner when the SC is locally and transiently inhibited.
source: In mice, detection of change in isolated visual stimuli is impaired in a space- and time-specific manner when the SC is locally and transiently inhibited (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The mouse SC is involved in hunting.
source: The mouse SC is also involved in hunting (Hoy et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2019) as well as defensive responses (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018) to visual stimuli that are clearly isolated from the background.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mouse SC is involved in defensive responses to visual stimuli that are clearly isolated from the background.
source: The mouse SC is also involved in hunting (Hoy et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2019) as well as defensive responses (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018) to visual stimuli that are clearly isolated from the background.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A growing number of experiments point towards a role for the SC in more complex processes that are usually associated with the cerebral cortex.
source: In recent years, a growing number of experiments point towards a role for the SC in more complex processes that are usually associated with the cerebral cortex (Krauzlis et al., 2013; Basso and May, 2017; Basso et al., 2021; Jun et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is not yet clear whether SC is also involved in detection of stimuli on a complex background.
source: It is, however, not yet clear whether SC is also involved in detection of stimuli on a complex background.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: When V1 is transiently silenced, mice are still able to detect stimuli that are defined by contrast on a homogeneous background.
source: When V1 is transiently silenced, mice are still able to detect stimuli that are defined by contrast on a homogeneous background, but they cannot detect texture-defined figures that only differ from the surrounding textured background by orientation (Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When V1 is transiently silenced, mice cannot detect texture-defined figures that only differ from the surrounding textured background by orientation.
source: When V1 is transiently silenced, mice are still able to detect stimuli that are defined by contrast on a homogeneous background, but they cannot detect texture-defined figures that only differ from the surrounding textured background by orientation (Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Models for detection of texture-defined figure stimuli focus on the visual cortex and presume that interactions within V1 enhance the neural response to the figure edges.
source: Models for detection of texture-defined figure stimuli focus on the visual cortex and presume that interactions within V1 enhance the neural response to the figure edges, and that higher cortical visual areas feed back to 'fill in' the neuronal representation of the figure in V1 (Roelfsema et al., 2002; Poort et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Higher cortical visual areas feed back to 'fill in' the neuronal representation of the figure in V1.
source: Models for detection of texture-defined figure stimuli focus on the visual cortex and presume that interactions within V1 enhance the neural response to the figure edges, and that higher cortical visual areas feed back to 'fill in' the neuronal representation of the figure in V1 (Roelfsema et al., 2002; Poort et al., 2012; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neurons in V1 of mice and primates respond more vigorously to image elements in their receptive fields that differ from the surrounding texture.
source: Indeed, neurons in V1 of mice and primates respond more vigorously to image elements in their receptive fields that differ from the surrounding texture (Lamme, 1995; Poort et al., 2012; Self et al., 2014; Li et al., 2018; Schnabel et al., 2018; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Figure-ground modulation depends on feedback from higher visual cortical areas.
source: This figure-ground modulation (FGM) depends on feedback from higher visual cortical areas, as was predicted by the models (Roelfsema et al., 2002; Keller et al., 2020; Pak et al., 2020; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ability to encode visual contextual effects is not exclusive to the visual cortex.
source: However, the ability to encode visual contextual effects is not exclusive to the visual cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is supported by subsequent citations.

claim: The superficial layers of the rodent SC (sSC) display orientation-tuned surround suppression.
source: The superficial layers of the rodent SC (sSC) have been shown to display orientation-tuned surround suppression (Girman and Lund, 2007; Ahmadlou et al., 2017; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2020): the responses of orientation-tuned neurons to an optimally oriented grating stimulus are attenuated when the surround contains a grating of the same orientation, whereas the responses are less suppressed or facilitated when the surround contains an orthogonal grating (Allman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The responses of orientation-tuned neurons in sSC to an optimally oriented grating stimulus are attenuated when the surround contains a grating of the same orientation.
source: The superficial layers of the rodent SC (sSC) have been shown to display orientation-tuned surround suppression (Girman and Lund, 2007; Ahmadlou et al., 2017; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2020): the responses of orientation-tuned neurons to an optimally oriented grating stimulus are attenuated when the surround contains a grating of the same orientation, whereas the responses are less suppressed or facilitated when the surround contains an orthogonal grating (Allman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The responses of orientation-tuned neurons in sSC are less suppressed or facilitated when the surround contains an orthogonal grating.
source: The superficial layers of the rodent SC (sSC) have been shown to display orientation-tuned surround suppression (Girman and Lund, 2007; Ahmadlou et al., 2017; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2020): the responses of orientation-tuned neurons to an optimally oriented grating stimulus are attenuated when the surround contains a grating of the same orientation, whereas the responses are less suppressed or facilitated when the surround contains an orthogonal grating (Allman et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Orientation-tuned surround suppression is thought to play an important role in object segregation.
source: This property is thought to play an important role in object segregation (Lamme, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The orientation-tuned surround suppression in sSC is computed independently of V1.
source: Interestingly, Ahmadlou et al., 2017 showed that the orientation-tuned surround suppression in sSC is computed independently of V1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Inhibiting the sSC reduces performance on a variety of figure detection tasks.
source: Here, we show that inhibiting the sSC reduces performance on a variety of figure detection tasks – indicating a role for the sSC in this behavior.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mouse SC contains a neural code for figure detection.
source: Furthermore, we use extracellular recordings in mice performing figure detection to show that mouse SC indeed contains a neural code for figure detection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recordings shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: A total of n=8 mice were used for the optogenetics experiments.
source: A total of n=8 mice were used for these experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: The mice typically performed 100–250 trials per session.
source: The mice typically performed 100–250 trials per session (one session per day, five sessions per week, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the recording period lasted for 2–5 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The recording period lasted for 2–5 months.
source: The mice typically performed 100–250 trials per session (one session per day, five sessions per week, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and the recording period lasted for 2–5 months (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For each of the three-figure detection tasks, the onset of the sSC inhibition significantly affected the accuracy of the mice.
source: For each of the three-figure detection tasks, the onset of the sSC inhibition significantly affected the accuracy of the mice (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A), p=0.005, p=0.027, and p=0.003 for the contrast, orientation, and phase task, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The optogenetic interference did not significantly influence the mice's licking rates.
source: The optogenetic interference did not significantly influence the mice's licking rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C) or reaction times (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is a control finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The optogenetic interference did not significantly influence the mice's reaction times.
source: The optogenetic interference did not significantly influence the mice's licking rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C) or reaction times (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This is a control finding supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The accuracies of the mice were decreased by the optogenetic manipulation of the sSC but typically were still above the chance level.
source: Although the accuracies of the mice were decreased by the optogenetic manipulation of the sSC, they typically were still above the chance level.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The incomplete silencing of the sSC might be related to the fact that accuracies were still above chance level.
source: This might be related to the incomplete silencing of the sSC, although it is also possible that the thalamocortical pathway is involved in figure detection in parallel to the sSC.
evidence: This is speculation about the interpretation of the results.

claim: It is possible that the thalamocortical pathway is involved in figure detection in parallel to the sSC.
source: This might be related to the incomplete silencing of the sSC, although it is also possible that the thalamocortical pathway is involved in figure detection in parallel to the sSC.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for the results.

claim: For the contrast task, the accuracy reached the half-maximal value when the laser onset was postponed to 99 ms (±8 ms).
source: For the contrast task, the accuracy reached the half-maximal value when we postponed the laser onset to 99 ms (±8 ms).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In the orientation task, the mice reached their half-maximum performance when the laser onset was postponed to 156 ms (±35 ms).
source: In the orientation and phase task, the mice reached their half-maximum performance when we postponed the laser onset to 156 ms (±35 ms) and 134 ms (±30 ms), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: In the phase task, the mice reached their half-maximum performance when the laser onset was postponed to 134 ms (±30 ms).
source: In the orientation and phase task, the mice reached their half-maximum performance when we postponed the laser onset to 156 ms (±35 ms) and 134 ms (±30 ms), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Short-lasting activity in the sSC suffices for the contrast detection task.
source: The data suggest that short-lasting activity in the sSC suffices for the contrast detection task, whereas orientation-and phase-defined object detection necessitate a longer phase of sSC activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the timing data of the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Orientation- and phase-defined object detection necessitate a longer phase of sSC activity.
source: The data suggest that short-lasting activity in the sSC suffices for the contrast detection task, whereas orientation-and phase-defined object detection necessitate a longer phase of sSC activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the timing data of the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Differences in processing time probably reflect differences in the encoding strategy of the brain for the different tasks rather than task difficulty.
source: Based on comparisons between the response accuracy and processing time of the mice in their experiments, Kirchberger et al., 2021 concluded that it is not likely that these differences depend on task difficulty for the mouse. Rather, they probably reflect differences in the encoding strategy of the brain for the different tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on a citation to prior research.

claim: Orientation- and phase-defined figures elicit more activity in the visual cortex of the mouse than the background image does.
source: Recent experiments have demonstrated that orientation- and phase-defined figures elicit more activity in the visual cortex of the mouse than the background image does; a phenomenon called figure-ground modulation (FGM) (Lamme, 1995; Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The mice could perform the tasks reliably above chance level during the recording sessions.
source: The mice could perform the tasks reliably above chance level during these recording sessions (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neural activity was recorded from five mice.
source: We recorded neural activity from five mice.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: Most neurons showed a short latency visual response.
source: Most neurons showed a short latency visual response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), although not all neurons in our data set were exclusively visually responsive and some appeared to respond to the movement of the lick spout (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for an extensive analysis of these).
evidence: This is an observation from the neural recording data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Not all neurons in the data set were exclusively visually responsive and some appeared to respond to the movement of the lick spout.
source: Most neurons showed a short latency visual response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), although not all neurons in our data set were exclusively visually responsive and some appeared to respond to the movement of the lick spout (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for an extensive analysis of these).
evidence: This is an observation from the neural recording data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For contrast-defined figures, significant FGM was found with an estimated onset of 67 ms.
source: In these visually responsive neurons, the contrast-defined figure elicited a strong response compared to the gray background, with an estimated onset of 67 ms (Figure 2H–J, left; p<0.05 from 68 to 99 ms in Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: For orientation-defined figures, significant FGM was found with an estimated onset of 75 ms.
source: For the orientation-defined figures, we also found significant FGM, with an estimated onset of 75 ms (Figure 2I–J, middle; p<0.05 from 84 to 129 ms in Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: When the figure was defined by a phase difference, FGM was not significant.
source: When the figure was defined by a phase difference, FGM was not significant (Figure 2I–J, right; p>0.05 for all time bins in Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The activity of sSC neurons elicited by contrast- and orientation-based figures is stronger than that elicited by a background.
source: We conclude that the activity of sSC neurons elicited by contrast- and orientation-based figures is stronger than that elicited by a background.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural recording data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The neural modulation in the contrast and orientation tasks could not be explained by eye movements or changes in pupil dilation.
source: As we had excluded trials with eye movements from the analysis (see methods section), the neural modulation in the contrast and orientation tasks could not be explained by eye movements or changes in pupil dilation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a control finding supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: For neurons with RFs on the edge of the figure stimulus, a significantly higher response for figure vs. ground was found in the orientation task.
source: For these neurons, we found a significantly higher response for figure vs. ground in the orientation task, but not in the phase task (Figure 3B; p<0.05 from 81 to 102 ms in the orientation task, p>0.05 for all time bins in the phase task, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For neurons with RFs on the edge of the figure stimulus, no significantly higher response for figure vs. ground was found in the phase task.
source: For these neurons, we found a significantly higher response for figure vs. ground in the orientation task, but not in the phase task (Figure 3B; p<0.05 from 81 to 102 ms in the orientation task, p>0.05 for all time bins in the phase task, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The phase-defined figure-ground stimulus did not cause a significantly enhanced population response in the sSC.
source: We conclude that the phase-defined figure-ground stimulus did not cause a significantly enhanced population response in the sSC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural recording data.

claim: For the orientation task, the decoder could detect the stimulus identity at a performance of around 75%.
source: For the orientation task, the decoder could detect the stimulus identity at a performance of around 75% (lowest p<0.001 at a time window 80–130 ms).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The decoder detected the phase stimulus identity above chance level in later time windows, after the peak of the visual response.
source: Interestingly, the decoder also detected the phase stimulus identity above chance level, more specifically in later time windows, after the peak of the visual response (lowest p<0.001 at time window 180–230 ms).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Visual information from both the orientation and the phase task is represented in the sSC.
source: These results are in line with the onset and relative strength of the figure-ground modulation for each task, and show that visual information from both the orientation and the phase task is represented in the sSC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the decoding analysis.

claim: The relative normalized weights were significantly higher for the orientation task compared to the phase task.
source: The relative normalized weights were significantly higher for the orientation task compared to the phase task.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of SVM model weights shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Some neurons may encode the phase-based figures by decreasing their firing rate, leading to negative relative weights.
source: This indicates that, whereas sSC neurons encode the orientation-based figures by increasing their firing rate, some neurons may indeed encode the phase-based figures by decreasing their firing rate, leading to negative relative weights.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of SVM model weights.

claim: For both orientation and phase tasks, the d-primes were significantly higher than the chance level in the time window with the best SVM decoding performance.
source: For both tasks, the d-primes were significantly higher than the chance level in the time window with the best SVM decoding performance (Figure 3F; p<0.001; and p<0.05 for orientation and phase, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the d-prime analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Although the average difference between figure vs. ground responses was small in the phase task, the variability of the neuronal responses was low enough for reliable decoding.
source: We conclude that although the average difference between figure vs. ground responses was small in the phase task, the variability of the neuronal responses was low enough for reliable decoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the d-prime and decoding analyses.

claim: The discriminability (d-prime) was significantly higher for hit trials than error trials.
source: The discriminability (d-prime) was significantly higher for hit trials than error trials (p=0.001), showing that activity in the sSC is reflected in the behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Activity in the sSC is reflected in the behavioral performance.
source: The discriminability (d-prime) was significantly higher for hit trials than error trials (p=0.001), showing that activity in the sSC is reflected in the behavioral performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the d-prime analysis comparing hits and errors.

claim: The difference in discriminability was mainly driven by the difference between hits and errors in the orientation task.
source: Post-hoc analysis showed that the difference in discriminability was mainly driven by the difference between hits and errors in the orientation task (Figure 4—source data 1; p=0.001; and p=0.303 for orientation and phase, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The superficial layers of superior colliculus are involved in detecting objects on a non-homogeneous background.
source: Our experiments show that the superficial layers of superior colliculus are involved in detecting objects on a non-homogeneous background and detecting objects based on figure contrast, orientation, and phase.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Neurons in sSC show an increased response to figure stimuli compared to ground stimuli in both the contrast and orientation task.
source: Indeed, neurons in sSC show an increased response to figure stimuli compared to ground stimuli in both the contrast and orientation task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the neural recording experiments.

claim: A significantly increased population response for phase-defined figures was not found.
source: We did not find a significantly increased population response for phase-defined figures, but a linear SVM decoder indicated that the response difference was consistent enough to decode the phase stimulus above chance level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the neural recording and decoding experiments.

claim: A linear SVM decoder indicated that the response difference was consistent enough to decode the phase stimulus above chance level.
source: We did not find a significantly increased population response for phase-defined figures, but a linear SVM decoder indicated that the response difference was consistent enough to decode the phase stimulus above chance level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the decoding experiments.

claim: sSC activity may contribute to the decision of the mouse.
source: The discriminability between figure- and ground responses was higher for hit trials than error trials, suggesting that sSC activity may contribute to the decision of the mouse.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the hit vs. error analysis.

claim: This study was aimed at the superficial part of SC (i.e. the stratum zonale, stratum griseum superficiale, and the stratum opticum).
source: This study was aimed at the superficial part of SC (i.e. the stratum zonale, stratum griseum superficiale, and the stratum opticum), although we cannot rule out the possibility that in some animals deeper parts of SC were recorded or were affected by optogenetics.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: This is one of only few studies that specifically inhibited the superficial part of SC bilaterally.
source: Interestingly, to our knowledge, this is one of only few studies that specifically inhibited the superficial part of SC bilaterally.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach.

claim: Most of the GABAergic neurons in the sSC are locally projecting.
source: Most of the GABAergic neurons in the sSC are also locally projecting, but there is a fraction of GABAergic neurons projecting out of the superior colliculus to the parabigeminal nucleus and the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN); the vLGN in particular (Gale and Murphy, 2014; Whyland et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There is a fraction of GABAergic neurons projecting out of the superior colliculus to the parabigeminal nucleus and the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: Most of the GABAergic neurons in the sSC are also locally projecting, but there is a fraction of GABAergic neurons projecting out of the superior colliculus to the parabigeminal nucleus and the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN); the vLGN in particular (Gale and Murphy, 2014; Whyland et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results suggest that superior colliculus is necessary not just for simple but also for relatively complex object detection.
source: Our results suggest that superior colliculus is necessary not just for simple but also for relatively complex object detection, when the figure does not stand out from the background by contrast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: SC is causally involved in detecting orientation change.
source: Previous experiments have already shown that the SC is causally involved in detecting orientation change (Wang et al., 2020), looming stimuli (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018), and detecting moving objects during hunting (Hoy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: SC is causally involved in detecting looming stimuli.
source: Previous experiments have already shown that the SC is causally involved in detecting orientation change (Wang et al., 2020), looming stimuli (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018), and detecting moving objects during hunting (Hoy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SC is causally involved in detecting moving objects during hunting.
source: Previous experiments have already shown that the SC is causally involved in detecting orientation change (Wang et al., 2020), looming stimuli (Evans et al., 2018; Shang et al., 2018), and detecting moving objects during hunting (Hoy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The stimuli showed a clear figure edge, due to the adaptation of the stimulus to mouse acuity.
source: Unlike commonly used stimuli for macaques, our stimuli showed a clear figure edge, due to the adaptation of the stimulus to mouse acuity.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental design.

claim: A linear decoder fed with simple cell-like inputs is able to perform the orientation task.
source: In line with this, it has been shown that a linear decoder fed with simple cell-like inputs is able to perform the orientation task (Luongo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A network fed with simple cell-like inputs failed to learn the phase task.
source: The same network failed to learn the phase task, but even the image of a phase-defined figure contains features that are not present in the background image, and could be solved by learning only local features.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: After training on a restricted training set, mice generalize over size, location, and orientation of the figure gratings.
source: Earlier experiments with the same stimuli in freely walking mice, however, suggested that after training on a restricted training set, mice generalize over size, location, and orientation of the figure gratings, and therefore, perform the task as if they detect the presence of an object (Schnabel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mice and rats have difficulty generalizing from luminance-defined objects to texture-defined objects.
source: Mice and rats have difficulty generalizing from luminance-defined objects to texture-defined objects (De Keyser et al., 2015; Khastkhodaei et al., 2016), but once they are acquainted with one set of texture-defined figures, they immediately generalize to other texture-orientations (De Keyser et al., 2015; Luongo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Once mice are acquainted with one set of texture-defined figures, they immediately generalize to other texture-orientations.
source: Mice and rats have difficulty generalizing from luminance-defined objects to texture-defined objects (De Keyser et al., 2015; Khastkhodaei et al., 2016), but once they are acquainted with one set of texture-defined figures, they immediately generalize to other texture-orientations (De Keyser et al., 2015; Luongo et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: At least some generalization for feature detection to object detection occurs in this task.
source: This suggests that at least some generalization for feature detection to object detection occurs in this task.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research.

claim: The accuracy of the mice did not decrease to chance level when inhibiting the sSC.
source: Interestingly, the accuracy of the mice did not decrease to chance level when inhibiting the sSC.
evidence: This is an observation from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Other brain areas contribute in parallel to the performance of this visual task.
source: This might be partially due to the incomplete silencing of sSC (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), but also suggests that other brain areas contribute in parallel to the performance of this visual task.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: Many studies have shown the involvement of mouse V1 in object detection.
source: Many studies have shown the involvement of mouse V1 in object detection (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Katzner et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mice can perform the contrast detection task above chance level when V1 is silenced.
source: Evidence that SC works in parallel to the visual cortex comes from the finding that mice can perform the contrast detection task above chance level when V1 is silenced (Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The detection of orientation-defined and phase-defined figures was abolished when V1 was silenced.
source: The detection of orientation-defined and phase-defined figures, however, was abolished when V1 was silenced (Kirchberger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The parallel processing stream through the superior colliculus does not suffice for detection of orientation-defined and phase-defined figures.
source: This suggests that the parallel processing stream through the superior colliculus does not suffice for detection of these more complex figures.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research.

claim: In V1, the half-maximum performance times were 62 ms, 101 ms, and 141 ms for detection based on contrast, orientation, and phase, respectively.
source: In V1, the corresponding half-maximum performance times were 62 ms, 101 ms, and 141 ms.
evidence: This is data from a cited prior study used for comparison.

claim: V1 performs a role in object detection at an earlier point in time than sSC for object detection based on contrast and orientation, but not phase.
source: The parsimonious interpretation of these findings is that V1 performs a role in object detection at an earlier point in time than sSC (for object detection based on contrast and orientation, but not phase).
evidence: This is an inference from comparing timing data between the current study and prior research.

claim: In V1, the onset times of the FGM for contrast, orientation, and phase were estimated at 43 ms, 75 ms, and 91 ms, respectively.
source: However, the onset times of the neural responses paint a slightly different picture: in V1, the onset times of the FGM for contrast, orientation, and phase were estimated at 43 ms, 75 ms, and 91 ms, respectively.
evidence: This is data from a cited prior study used for comparison.

claim: The onset times recorded in sSC were 67 and 75ms for contrast and orientation stimuli.
source: The onset times we recorded in sSC were 67 and 75ms for contrast and orientation stimuli, and a non-significant result for the phase stimuli.
evidence: This is data from the current study.

claim: The onset time of the modulation in sSC suggests that it is computed independently of V1.
source: Although our estimates of the onset time of FGM are not precise enough to fully rule out the possibility that modulation of V1 is transferred to sSC through the direct projection, the onset time of the modulation in sSC suggests that it is computed independently of V1.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing timing data.

claim: Orientation-dependent surround suppression in sSC increases if V1 is inhibited.
source: This independency of V1 has also been shown for orientation-dependent surround suppression in sSC (Girman and Lund, 2007), which even increases if V1 is inhibited (Ahmadlou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The medial visual areas could be silenced without a drop in performance in a simple visual detection task.
source: Goldbach et al., 2021 showed that these medial visual areas could be silenced without a drop in performance in a simple visual detection task.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Geniculate projections to medial visual areas are not likely to be of major importance in the figure detection task.
source: Therefore, it does not seem likely that these geniculate projections would be of major importance in the figure detection task.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited prior research.

claim: Mouse sSC provides a significant contribution to the processing of complex visual stimuli.
source: These results fit in with the growing number of studies that show mouse sSC provides a significant contribution to the processing of complex visual stimuli (Ahmadlou et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The superior colliculus (or the optic tectum in non-mammalian species) is a brain area conserved across vertebrate evolution.
source: The superior colliculus (or the optic tectum in non-mammalian species) is a brain area conserved across vertebrate evolution (Isa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC in their received retinal inputs.
source: Even though clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC, for example in their received retinal inputs (Ito and Feldheim, 2018), representation of visual features (Wang et al., 2010; Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen and Hafed, 2018), and more generally the animals' strategies for visual segmentation (Luongo et al., 2023), many functions of sSC are shared between rodents and primates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC in their representation of visual features.
source: Even though clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC, for example in their received retinal inputs (Ito and Feldheim, 2018), representation of visual features (Wang et al., 2010; Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen and Hafed, 2018), and more generally the animals' strategies for visual segmentation (Luongo et al., 2023), many functions of sSC are shared between rodents and primates.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clear differences exist between mouse and primate in their strategies for visual segmentation.
source: Even though clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC, for example in their received retinal inputs (Ito and Feldheim, 2018), representation of visual features (Wang et al., 2010; Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen and Hafed, 2018), and more generally the animals' strategies for visual segmentation (Luongo et al., 2023), many functions of sSC are shared between rodents and primates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Many functions of sSC are shared between rodents and primates.
source: Even though clear differences exist between mouse and primate sSC, for example in their received retinal inputs (Ito and Feldheim, 2018), representation of visual features (Wang et al., 2010; Ahmadlou and Heimel, 2015; Chen and Hafed, 2018), and more generally the animals' strategies for visual segmentation (Luongo et al., 2023), many functions of sSC are shared between rodents and primates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Shared functions of sSC between rodents and primates include saliency mapping.
source: Some of these include saliency mapping (White et al., 2017; Barchini et al., 2018), spatial attention (Krauzlis et al., 2013; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018; Hu and Dan, 2022; Wang et al., 2022), and orienting behavior (Boehnke and Munoz, 2008; Masullo et al., 2019; Zahler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Shared functions of sSC between rodents and primates include spatial attention.
source: Some of these include saliency mapping (White et al., 2017; Barchini et al., 2018), spatial attention (Krauzlis et al., 2013; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018; Hu and Dan, 2022; Wang et al., 2022), and orienting behavior (Boehnke and Munoz, 2008; Masullo et al., 2019; Zahler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Shared functions of sSC between rodents and primates include orienting behavior.
source: Some of these include saliency mapping (White et al., 2017; Barchini et al., 2018), spatial attention (Krauzlis et al., 2013; Wang and Krauzlis, 2018; Hu and Dan, 2022; Wang et al., 2022), and orienting behavior (Boehnke and Munoz, 2008; Masullo et al., 2019; Zahler et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Primate sSC shows object coding.
source: This, together with recent work showing object coding in the primate (Griggs et al., 2018; Bogadhi and Hafed, 2022), suggests that also primate sSC contributes to visual processing in more various and complex ways than anticipated based on previous work.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Primate sSC contributes to visual processing in more various and complex ways than anticipated based on previous work.
source: This, together with recent work showing object coding in the primate (Griggs et al., 2018; Bogadhi and Hafed, 2022), suggests that also primate sSC contributes to visual processing in more various and complex ways than anticipated based on previous work.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and cited prior research.
